original.title: Exact values from exponential definitions
original.question_html:
(a)[3]

Use exponential definitions to find the exact values of \(\sinh(\ln4)\), \(\cosh(\ln4)\) and \(\tanh(-\ln4)\).

(b)[2]

Prove directly from the definitions that \((\cosh x+\sinh x)(\cosh x-\sinh x)=1\) for every real \(x\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use \(e^{\ln4}=4\) and \(e^{-\ln4}=\frac14\).

(b)

Simplify the two factors separately.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(\frac{15}{8},\ \frac{17}{8},\ -\frac{15}{17}\), respectively.

(b)

\(\cosh x+\sinh x=e^x\) and \(\cosh x-\sinh x=e^{-x}\), so their product is 1.
original.solution_html:
(a)

The definitions give

\[\sinh(\ln4)=\frac{4-\frac14}{2}=\frac{15}{8},\qquad \cosh(\ln4)=\frac{4+\frac14}{2}=\frac{17}{8}.\]

For the negative argument, interchange the two exponentials in the numerator of sinh; cosh is unchanged. Thus

\[\tanh(-\ln4)=\frac{-15/8}{17/8}=-\frac{15}{17}.\]

(b)

Adding and subtracting the exponential definitions gives

\[\cosh x+\sinh x=e^x,\qquad \cosh x-\sinh x=e^{-x}.\]

Their product is \(e^xe^{-x}=1\). Both definitions are valid for every real \(x\).

original.title: Recovering the hyperbolic ratios
original.question_html:
It is given that \(a>0\) and \(\tanh a=\frac5{13}\).

(a)[4]

Find the exact values of \(\sinh a,\cosh a,\operatorname{sech}a,\operatorname{cosech}a\) and \(\operatorname{coth}a\).

(b)[2]

Hence find \(a\) in logarithmic form.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Write \(\sinh a=5u\), \(\cosh a=13u\), and use \(\cosh^2a-\sinh^2a=1\).

(b)

Use \(e^a=\cosh a+\sinh a\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(\sinh a=5u\) and \(\cosh a=13u\). Since cosh is positive, \(u>0\). The identity yields

\[(13u)^2-(5u)^2=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad144u^2=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u=\frac1{12}.\]

Hence \(\sinh a=5/12\) and \(\cosh a=13/12\). Taking the reciprocals of cosh, sinh and tanh gives \(12/13\), \(12/5\) and \(13/5\), respectively.

(b)

\[e^a=\frac{13}{12}+\frac5{12}=\frac32.\]

Taking logarithms gives \(a=\ln(3/2)>0\), consistent with the condition.

original.title: An equation and an inequality
original.question_html:
(a)[4]

Solve \(3\cosh x-2\sinh x=3\), giving all real solutions in exact form.

(b)[2]

Solve \(3\cosh x-2\sinh x<3\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Set \(u=e^x>0\).

(b)

The multiplier \(2e^x\) is always positive.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Using exponentials,

\[3\cosh x-2\sinh x=\frac{e^x+5e^{-x}}2.\]

Put \(u=e^x>0\). Multiplying by \(2u\) gives

\[u^2-6u+5=(u-1)(u-5)=0.\]

Both values of \(u\) are positive, so both are allowed. Therefore \(x=0\) or \(x=\ln5\).

(b)

The inequality is equivalent to \((u-1)(u-5)<0\), because multiplying by \(2u>0\) preserves its direction. Thus \(1<u<5\). Since the logarithm is increasing,

\[0<x<\ln5.\]

original.title: A ratio that simplifies
original.question_html:
(a)[3]

Starting from exponential definitions, show that \(\frac{\sinh 2x}{\cosh x}=e^x-e^{-x}\).

(b)[3]

Hence solve \(\sinh2x=3\cosh x\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Factor \(e^{2x}-e^{-2x}\).

(b)

Use the identity, then solve a quadratic in \(e^x\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{\sinh2x}{\cosh x}=\frac{e^{2x}-e^{-2x}}{e^x+e^{-x}}=\frac{(e^x-e^{-x})(e^x+e^{-x})}{e^x+e^{-x}}=e^x-e^{-x}.\]

The cancelled factor is strictly positive, so the identity is valid for all real \(x\).

(b)

As \(\cosh x>0\), division loses no solutions. Part (a) gives \(e^x-e^{-x}=3\). With \(u=e^x>0\),

\[u^2-3u-1=0,\qquad u=\frac{3\pm\sqrt{13}}2.\]

Only the positive root is admissible. Thus \(x=\ln((3+\sqrt{13})/2)\).

original.stem_html: A real number \(x\) satisfies \(\cosh x+\sinh x=7(\cosh x-\sinh x)\).
original.question_html:

\[\tanh x=\frac{7-1}{7+1}=\frac34.\]

Also \(e^{4x}=49\), so

\[\tanh2x=\frac{49-1}{49+1}=\frac{24}{25}.\]

original.title: A minimum without differentiation
original.question_html:
Let \(f(x)=2e^x+8e^{-x}\), for \(x\in\mathbb R\).

(a)[3]

Write \(f(x)\) in the form \(A\cosh(x-b)\), where \(A>0\).

(b)[1]

State the minimum value of \(f\) and where it occurs.

(c)[2]

Solve \(f(x)=10\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Compare the coefficients of \(e^x\) and \(e^{-x}\).

(b)

The least value of cosh is 1.

(c)

Use \(\cosh(\ln2)=5/4\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[A\cosh(x-b)=\frac{Ae^{-b}}2e^x+\frac{Ae^b}2e^{-x}.\]

Matching coefficients gives \(Ae^{-b}=4\) and \(Ae^b=16\). Multiplication gives \(A^2=64\), so \(A=8\). Then \(e^b=2\), so \(b=\ln2\).

(b)

Since \(\cosh u\ge1\), with equality only at \(u=0\), the minimum is \(8\), attained at \(x=\ln2\).

(c)

The equation becomes \(\cosh(x-\ln2)=5/4\). Thus \(x-\ln2=\pm\ln2\), giving \(x=0\) or \(x=\ln4\).

original.title: The sum of two logarithmic roots
original.question_html:
(a)[4]

Solve \(4\cosh x+\sinh x=7\), giving both answers in logarithmic form.

(b)[2]

Without approximating either root, find their sum and determine its sign.
original.hint_html:
(a)

The exponential equation has two positive roots.

(b)

The product of the two exponential roots is \(3/5\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(u=e^x>0\). Then

\[\frac{5u+3/u}{2}=7\quad\Longrightarrow\quad5u^2-14u+3=0.\]

The roots are \(u=(7\pm\sqrt{34})/5\). Both are positive because \(7>\sqrt{34}\). Taking logarithms gives the stated two values.

(b)

If the roots in \(x\) are \(x_1,x_2\), then

\[x_1+x_2=\ln(e^{x_1}e^{x_2})=\ln\frac35.\]

This is negative since \(0<3/5<1\).

original.title: A parameter and an open range
original.question_html:
Define \(f(x)=\frac{e^{-x}}{\cosh x}\), for real \(x\).

(a)[3]

Show that \(f(x)=1-\tanh x\), and state its range.

(b)[3]

Find all real values of \(k\) for which \(f(x)=k\) has a real solution, and find that solution in terms of \(k\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Write \(e^{-x}=\cosh x-\sinh x\).

(b)

Use \(f(x)=2/(1+e^{2x})\).
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(f(x)=1-\tanh x\), with range \((0,2)\).

(b)

\(0<k<2\), with the unique solution \(x=\frac12\ln\frac{2-k}{k}\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

Dividing \(e^{-x}=\cosh x-\sinh x\) by the positive number \(\cosh x\) gives \(f(x)=1-\tanh x\). Since \(-1<\tanh x<1\), the range is \(0<f(x)<2\). Neither endpoint is attained.

(b)

\[f(x)=\frac{2}{1+e^{2x}}=k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^{2x}=\frac{2-k}{k}.\]

The right-hand side is positive exactly when \(0<k<2\). For each such \(k\), the exponential equation has one real solution,

\[x=\frac12\ln\frac{2-k}{k}.\]

original.title: A translated hyperbolic sine graph
original.question_html:
The curve \(C\) has equation \(y=\sinh(2x)-1\).

(a)[4]

Sketch \(C\). State its domain and range, label both axis intercepts in exact form, and identify its centre of symmetry.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Apply a horizontal compression and a vertical translation to \(y=\sinh x\).
original.answer_html:
(a)

Domain and range: \(\mathbb R\). Intercepts \((0,-1)\) and \((\tfrac12\ln(1+\sqrt2),0)\). Centre \((0,-1)\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

The function \(\sinh(2x)\) is odd, continuous and strictly increasing, with all real values. Subtracting 1 gives centre of symmetry \((0,-1)\), while the domain and range remain \(\mathbb R\).

At \(x=0\), \(y=-1\). For the horizontal-axis intercept,

\[\sinh(2x)=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad2x=\ln(1+\sqrt2).\]

The sketch is an increasing S-shaped curve through these intercepts. It has no horizontal or vertical asymptote.

original.title: A shifted hyperbolic cosine graph
original.question_html:
A curve has equation \(y=3\cosh(x+\ln2)-4\).

(a)[5]

Sketch the curve, stating its minimum point, its range and all axis intercepts in exact form.
original.hint_html:
(a)

The minimum occurs when the argument of cosh is zero.
original.solution_html:
(a)

The argument of cosh is zero at \(x=-\ln2\), where \(y=3-4=-1\). Thus the curve is symmetric about \(x=-\ln2\), and its range is \([-1,\infty)\).

At \(x=0\), \(\cosh(\ln2)=5/4\), so \(y=-1/4\). Horizontal-axis intersections satisfy

\[\cosh(x+\ln2)=\frac43.\]

There are two arguments, \(\pm\cosh^{-1}(4/3)\), giving

\[x=-\ln2\pm\ln\frac{4+\sqrt7}{3}.\]

Both arms of the U-shaped curve rise without bound.

Let \(y=2\tanh(3x)-1\).

original.title: A reciprocal graph and an inequality
original.question_html:
The function \(g\) is defined by \(g(x)=\operatorname{sech}(x-1)\).

(a)[3]

Sketch the graph. State its range, maximum point and any asymptotes.

(b)[3]

Solve \(g(x)\ge\frac12\), giving exact endpoints.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use \(\operatorname{sech}u=1/\cosh u\).

(b)

Invert the inequality using the positivity of cosh.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Since \(\cosh(x-1)\ge1\), its reciprocal lies in \((0,1]\). Equality \(g=1\) occurs at \(x=1\). The graph is positive and symmetric about \(x=1\), and tends to zero at both ends. There are no vertical asymptotes or horizontal-axis intercepts.

(b)

Because cosh is positive,

\[\frac1{\cosh(x-1)}\ge\frac12\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\cosh(x-1)\le2.\]

By symmetry and monotonicity of cosh on \([0,\infty)\), \(|x-1|\le\cosh^{-1}2=\ln(2+\sqrt3)\). Hence the required closed interval is as stated.

original.title: Hyperbolic cosecant
original.question_html:
A curve has equation \(y=\operatorname{cosech}(2x)\).

(a)[3]

Sketch the curve, stating its domain, range, symmetry and asymptotes.

(b)[3]

Find the point on the curve whose \(y\)-coordinate is \(-\frac43\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Take the reciprocal of sinh, keeping its sign.

(b)

The corresponding sinh value is the reciprocal of \(-4/3\).
original.answer_html:
(a)

Domain and range \(\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\); odd symmetry; asymptotes \(x=0\), \(y=0\).

(b)

\(\left(-\frac12\ln2,-\frac43\right)\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

The denominator \(\sinh(2x)\) vanishes only at \(x=0\), so that value is excluded and \(x=0\) is a vertical asymptote. The reciprocal is never zero, but tends to zero as \(|x|\to\infty\); thus \(y=0\) is a horizontal asymptote. The graph is odd, with one positive branch for \(x>0\) and one negative branch for \(x<0\). Each nonzero real output occurs.

(b)

\[\operatorname{cosech}(2x)=-\frac43\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\sinh(2x)=-\frac34.\]

Since \(\sinh(\ln2)=3/4\) and sinh is odd and one-to-one, \(2x=-\ln2\). Therefore the point is \((-\tfrac12\ln2,-4/3)\).

original.title: A displaced coth curve
original.question_html:
The curve \(C\) has equation \(y=\operatorname{coth}(x+\ln2)\).

(a)[4]

Sketch \(C\). State its domain, range, asymptotes and vertical-axis intercept.

(b)[2]

Solve \(\operatorname{coth}(x+\ln2)=2\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

The pole of coth moves with its argument; its limiting values remain unchanged.

(b)

Use the exponential definition of coth.
original.solution_html:
(a)

The denominator vanishes when \(x+\ln2=0\), giving vertical asymptote \(x=-\ln2\). On the right branch coth decreases from \(+\infty\) towards 1; on the left it decreases from values near \(-1\) towards \(-\infty\). The horizontal asymptotes are \(y=1\) and \(y=-1\), neither attained.

At \(x=0\),

\[\operatorname{coth}(\ln2)=\frac{5/4}{3/4}=\frac53.\]

The two stated intervals form the range.

(b)

With \(u=x+\ln2\),

\[\frac{e^{2u}+1}{e^{2u}-1}=2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^{2u}=3.\]

Thus \(u=\tfrac12\ln3>0\), and \(x=\tfrac12\ln3-\ln2\). This lies to the right of the vertical asymptote.

original.title: An absolute value and the number of intersections
original.stem_html: The function \(h(x)=|\sinh x|-1\) is defined for all real \(x\).
original.question_html:
The function \(h(x)=|\sinh x|-1\) is defined for all real \(x\).

(a)[3]

Sketch \(y=h(x)\), marking its minimum point and axis intercepts.

(b)[3]

For each real \(k\), state the number of distinct solutions of \(h(x)=k\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

First reflect the negative part of sinh above the horizontal axis, then translate down.

(b)

Compare the horizontal line with the minimum height.
original.answer_html:
(a)

Minimum \((0,-1)\); zeros \(x=\pm\ln(1+\sqrt2)\); even symmetry.

(b)

No solutions if \(k<-1\); one if \(k=-1\); two if \(k>-1\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

The graph of \(|\sinh x|\) is even and is zero only at \(x=0\). Therefore \(h\) has minimum \(-1\) there, and is symmetric about the vertical axis. Its two branches meet in a corner at \((0,-1)\). The horizontal-axis intercepts satisfy \(|\sinh x|=1\), hence \(x=\pm\ln(1+\sqrt2)\).

(b)

The equation is \(|\sinh x|=k+1\). A negative right-hand side is impossible. If it is zero, \(x=0\) is the only solution. If it is positive, sinh being odd and strictly increasing gives exactly one positive and one negative solution. This proves all three cases, including the boundary.

(c)

The asymptotes give \(D-A=-2\) and \(D+A=6\). Adding yields \(D=2\), then \(A=4\). The centre has horizontal coordinate \(h\), so \(h=1\).

original.title: An addition identity and exact evaluation
original.question_html:
(a)[4]

Starting from exponential definitions, prove \(\cosh(u+v)=\cosh u\cosh v+\sinh u\sinh v\).

(b)[2]

Use this identity to evaluate \(\cosh(\ln2+\ln3)\) from the separate values at \(\ln2\) and \(\ln3\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Expand the two products on the right before adding.

(b)

Find each sinh and cosh from its exponential definition.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Substitution into the right-hand side gives

\[\frac14\big[(e^u+e^{-u})(e^v+e^{-v})+(e^u-e^{-u})(e^v-e^{-v})\big].\]

Expanding, the terms \(e^{u-v}\) and \(e^{-u+v}\) cancel, leaving

\[\frac14(2e^{u+v}+2e^{-u-v})=\frac12(e^{u+v}+e^{-(u+v)})=\cosh(u+v).\]

No restrictions on the real numbers \(u,v\) were needed.

(b)

The four needed values are \(\cosh\ln2=5/4\), \(\sinh\ln2=3/4\), \(\cosh\ln3=5/3\), \(\sinh\ln3=4/3\). Hence

\[\cosh(\ln2+\ln3)=\frac54\frac53+\frac34\frac43=\frac{25+12}{12}=\frac{37}{12}.\]

original.title: A double-angle equation for tanh
original.question_html:
(a)[3]

Prove that \(\tanh2x=\frac{2\tanh x}{1+\tanh^2x}\).

(b)[4]

Hence solve \(\tanh2x=\frac32\tanh x\), giving every real solution in logarithmic form.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the double-angle formulae for sinh and cosh, then divide by \(\cosh^2x\).

(b)

Do not cancel \(\tanh x\) before checking whether it is zero.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Using \(\sinh2x=2\sinh x\cosh x\) and \(\cosh2x=\cosh^2x+\sinh^2x\),

\[\tanh2x=\frac{2\sinh x\cosh x}{\cosh^2x+\sinh^2x}=\frac{2\tanh x}{1+\tanh^2x}.\]

Division by \(\cosh^2x\) is valid for all real \(x\).

(b)

Put \(t=\tanh x\), so \(-1<t<1\). Then

\[\frac{2t}{1+t^2}=\frac32t\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t(1-3t^2)=0.\]

Thus \(t=0\) or \(t=\pm1/\sqrt3\); all three are within the range of tanh. Since tanh is one-to-one,

\[x=0\quad\text{or}\quad x=\pm\frac12\ln\frac{\sqrt3+1}{\sqrt3-1}=\pm\frac12\ln(2+\sqrt3).\]

Keeping the factor \(t\) ensures that the solution \(x=0\) is not lost.

original.title: A half-angle quotient
original.question_html:
(a)[3]

For \(x\ne0\), prove \(\frac{\cosh x+1}{\sinh x}=\operatorname{coth}\frac x2\).

(b)[3]

Hence solve \(\frac{\cosh x+1}{\sinh x}=3\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Express the numerator and denominator using half-arguments.

(b)

Convert coth of the half-argument into an expression involving \(e^x\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

The double-angle identities give

\[\cosh x+1=2\cosh^2\frac x2,\qquad \sinh x=2\sinh\frac x2\cosh\frac x2.\]

Therefore their quotient is \(\cosh(x/2)/\sinh(x/2)=\operatorname{coth}(x/2)\). The restriction \(x\ne0\) ensures the denominator is nonzero.

\[\frac{e^x+1}{e^x-1}=3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^x+1=3e^x-3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^x=2.\]

Thus \(x=\ln2\), which is nonzero and satisfies the original equation.

original.question_html:
(a)[4]

Starting from exponential definitions, prove \(\cosh3x=4\cosh^3x-3\cosh x\).

(b)[3]

\[x=\pm\cosh^{-1}\sqrt2=\pm\ln(1+\sqrt2).\]

(a)[2]

original.title: A difference identity and monotonicity
original.question_html:
(a)[4]

Prove that \(\tanh(x+a)-\tanh x=\frac{\sinh a}{\cosh(x+a)\cosh x}\). Hence explain why tanh is strictly increasing on \(\mathbb R\).

(b)[2]

Given \(\tanh u=\frac13\) and \(\tanh v=\frac12\), find \(\tanh(u+v)\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Combine the fractions and use the sinh subtraction identity.

(b)

Divide the addition formula for sinh by that for cosh.
original.answer_html:
(a)

The displayed identity holds; if \(a>0\), its right-hand side is positive.

(b)

\(\tanh(u+v)=\frac57\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

Combining the two fractions gives numerator

\[\sinh(x+a)\cosh x-\sinh x\cosh(x+a)=\sinh a.\]

(b)

The addition formula is

\[\tanh(u+v)=\frac{\tanh u+\tanh v}{1+\tanh u\tanh v}=\frac{1/3+1/2}{1+1/6}=\frac57.\]

original.title: An inadmissible quadratic root
original.question_html:
(a)[5]

Solve \(2\sinh^2x-5\cosh x+1=0\), giving all real solutions in exact logarithmic form.

\[x=\pm\cosh^{-1}C=\pm\ln(C+\sqrt{C^2-1}).\]

Both solve the original equation; there are no others.

original.question_html:
Define \(F(x)=5\cosh x-3\sinh x\), for all real \(x\).

(a)[3]

Show that \(F(x)=4\cosh(x-\ln2)\).

(b)[3]

(b)

(c)

(a)

\(F(x)=4\cosh(x-\ln2)\).

(b)

(c)

original.stem_html: The function \(f(x)=\cosh(2x-1)\) is to be restricted to a domain of the form \([a,\infty)\).
original.question_html:
The function \(f(x)=\cosh(2x-1)\) is to be restricted to a domain of the form \([a,\infty)\).

(a)[2]

Find the least value of \(a\) for which \(f\) is one-to-one, and state its range for this domain.

(b)[3]

For this restriction, find \(f^{-1}(x)\) and state the domain and range of \(f^{-1}\).

(c)[1]

Find \(f^{-1}(5/4)\) exactly.

(a)

(b)

The restricted argument \(2x-1\) is nonnegative.

(c)

original.solution_html:
(a)

The graph is symmetric about \(x=1/2\). If \(a<1/2\), the domain includes points on both sides of the minimum with the same value of cosh, so it is not one-to-one. On \([1/2,\infty)\) it is strictly increasing. Thus the least \(a\) is \(1/2\), and the range is \([1,\infty)\).

(b)

Write \(y=\cosh(2x-1)\), with \(2x-1\ge0\). The principal inverse gives \(2x-1=\cosh^{-1}y\). Therefore

\[f^{-1}(x)=\frac{1+\cosh^{-1}x}{2}.\]

The inverse domain is the original range \([1,\infty)\), and its range is the original restricted domain \([1/2,\infty)\).

(c)

Since the principal value \(\cosh^{-1}(5/4)=\ln2\), substitution yields \((1+\ln2)/2\).

original.title: Inverting a translated sinh function
original.question_html:
Let \(f(x)=2\sinh(x-1)+3\), for \(x\in\mathbb R\).

(a)[3]

Find \(f^{-1}(x)\), stating its domain and range.

(b)[2]

Solve \(f^{-1}(x)=1+\ln2\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Undo the vertical transformations before applying inverse sinh.

(b)

Apply \(f\) to both sides, or use the inverse formula.
original.solution_html:
(a)

From \(y=2\sinh(x-1)+3\), obtain \(\sinh(x-1)=(y-3)/2\). Since sinh is one-to-one and has range \(\mathbb R\),

\[x=1+\sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{y-3}{2}\right).\]

Interchanging the variable names gives the stated inverse. Both its domain and range are all real numbers.

(b)

\[\sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{x-3}{2}\right)=\ln2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{x-3}{2}=\frac34.\]

Thus \(x=3+3/2=9/2\).

original.title: The domain of an inverse tanh transformation
original.question_html:
Define \(f(x)=3\tanh(2x)+1\), for real \(x\).

(a)[3]

Find an expression for \(f^{-1}(x)\).

(b)[2]

State the domain and range of \(f^{-1}\).

(c)[2]

Solve \(f^{-1}(x)<0\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Isolate tanh and remember to divide its argument by 2.

(b)

Tanh never attains either endpoint of its range.

(c)

Inverse tanh is increasing and is zero when its argument is zero.
original.solution_html:
(a)

If \(y=3\tanh(2x)+1\), then \(\tanh(2x)=(y-1)/3\). Applying the inverse gives \(2x=\tanh^{-1}((y-1)/3)\). Thus

\[f^{-1}(x)=\frac12\tanh^{-1}\left(\frac{x-1}{3}\right).\]

(b)

The original range follows from \(-1<\tanh(2x)<1\): it is \(-2<f(x)<4\). This becomes the inverse domain. The original domain is all real numbers, so the inverse range is \(\mathbb R\).

(c)

Within the inverse domain, \(\tanh^{-1}((x-1)/3)<0\) precisely when \((x-1)/3<0\). Combining \(x<1\) with \(-2<x<4\) gives \(-2<x<1\).

original.question_html:
(a)[3]

Simplify \(\sinh(\sinh^{-1}(3x-2))\) and \(\cosh(\sinh^{-1}x)\), stating the real domain of each expression.

(b)[3]

Hence simplify \(\tanh(\sinh^{-1}x)\) and solve \(\tanh(\sinh^{-1}x)=\frac35\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

For the second expression put \(u=\sinh^{-1}x\) and use the fundamental identity.

(b)

Use the quotient sinh/cosh, and check the sign before squaring.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(3x-2\) and \(\sqrt{1+x^2}\); both are defined for all real \(x\).

(b)

\(\tanh(\sinh^{-1}x)=\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\); solution \(x=\frac34\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

Sinh and its inverse are mutually inverse on \(\mathbb R\), so the first expression is \(3x-2\).

For the second, put \(u=\sinh^{-1}x\). Then \(\sinh u=x\), so \(\cosh^2u=1+x^2\). Since \(\cosh u>0\),

\[\cosh(\sinh^{-1}x)=\sqrt{1+x^2}.\]

Inverse sinh has all-real domain, so both expressions are defined for every real \(x\).

(b)

The quotient gives \(x/\sqrt{1+x^2}\). The equation forces \(x>0\). Squaring,

\[\frac{x^2}{1+x^2}=\frac9{25}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad16x^2=9.\]

Only \(x=3/4\) has the required positive sign. Direct substitution gives \((3/4)/(5/4)=3/5\).

original.title: Why the principal inverse produces a modulus
original.question_html:
(a)[3]

Write \(\cosh^{-1}(\cosh(2x-3))\) as a piecewise expression without hyperbolic functions.

(b)[2]

Hence solve \(\cosh^{-1}(\cosh(2x-3))=5\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

The principal inverse cosh returns a nonnegative value.

(b)

Solve both linear equations arising from the modulus.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Cosh is even. For a real \(u\), \(\cosh u=\cosh|u|\), and \(|u|\ge0\) lies on the principal inverse branch. Therefore \(\cosh^{-1}(\cosh u)=|u|\), not necessarily \(u\). Taking \(u=2x-3\), the sign changes at \(x=3/2\), giving the stated piecewise formula.

(b)

The equation is \(|2x-3|=5\), so \(2x-3=5\) or \(2x-3=-5\). These give \(x=4\) and \(x=-1\). Both are admissible in the original all-real domain.

original.title: Inverse is not reciprocal
original.question_html:
(a)[3]

Simplify \(\tanh^{-1}(\tanh x)\) and \(\tanh(\tanh^{-1}x)\), stating the real domain of each composition. Explain why \(\tanh^{-1}x\) is not the same as \(\operatorname{coth}x\).

(b)[3]

Solve \(\tanh^{-1}(2x)=\ln2\), checking the domain.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Distinguish the inverse function from the reciprocal value.

(b)

First require \(-1<2x<1\).
original.answer_html:
(a)

The first equals \(x\) for all real \(x\); the second equals \(x\) only for \(-1<x<1\). Coth is \(1/\tanh x\), not inverse tanh.

(b)

\(x=\frac3{10}\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

Tanh maps \(\mathbb R\) bijectively onto \((-1,1)\). Thus applying inverse tanh after tanh gives the original real input. In the reverse order, the inner inverse tanh is defined only on \((-1,1)\), and on that domain the result is again \(x\).

The superscript \(-1\) in inverse-function notation means undoing a function. The reciprocal is \(1/\tanh x=\operatorname{coth}x\), defined for \(x\ne0\), and has a different domain and meaning.

(b)

The domain is \(-1/2<x<1/2\). Applying tanh,

\[2x=\tanh(\ln2)=\frac{4-1}{4+1}=\frac35.\]

Hence \(x=3/10\), which lies in the required domain.

original.title: A translated inverse-sinh graph
original.question_html:
A curve has equation \(y=\sinh^{-1}(x+1)-\ln2\).

(a)[5]

Sketch the curve. State its domain and range, its centre of symmetry, and its exact axis intercepts.

\[y=\sinh^{-1}1-\ln2=\ln\frac{1+\sqrt2}{2}.\]

original.title: The endpoint of inverse cosh
original.question_html:
Consider \(y=\cosh^{-1}(x-2)\), using the principal inverse.

(a)[4]

State its domain and range, sketch the curve and describe its relationship to a suitable restricted cosh graph.

(b)[2]

Find the point with \(y=\ln3\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Inverse cosh requires its argument to be at least 1.

(b)

Apply cosh to the equation.
original.answer_html:
(a)

Domain \([3,\infty)\); range \([0,\infty)\); endpoint \((3,0)\). It is the reflection of \(y=\cosh x+2\), \(x\ge0\), in \(y=x\).

(b)

\(\left(\frac{11}{3},\ln3\right)\).

The argument condition is \(x-2\ge1\), so \(x\ge3\). The principal inverse returns \(y\ge0\). At the endpoint, \(\cosh^{-1}1=0\), giving \((3,0)\).

(b)

\(\cosh^{-1}(x-2)=\ln3\) gives \(x-2=\cosh(\ln3)=5/3\). Thus \(x=11/3\), which is in the domain, and the point is \((11/3,\ln3)\).

original.title: Deriving the logarithmic form of inverse sinh
original.question_html:
(a)[4]

Starting with \(y=\sinh^{-1}x\), derive a logarithmic expression for \(y\) and explain why it is valid for every real \(x\).

(b)[2]

Hence solve \(\sinh^{-1}(2x-1)=\ln3\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Solve a quadratic in \(e^y\), which must be positive.

(b)

Exponentiate the derived expression, or apply sinh.
original.solution_html:
(a)

From \(x=\sinh y\),

\[2x=e^y-e^{-y}.\]

Let \(u=e^y>0\). Multiplication by \(u\) gives \(u^2-2xu-1=0\), so \(u=x\pm\sqrt{x^2+1}\). Since \(\sqrt{x^2+1}>|x|\), the plus choice is positive and the minus choice negative for every real \(x\). Therefore

\[y=\ln(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}).\]

The logarithm's argument is strictly positive for all real \(x\), establishing the domain as well as the branch.

(b)

Applying sinh gives \(2x-1=\sinh(\ln3)=4/3\). Hence \(2x=7/3\), so \(x=7/6\). There is no additional domain restriction.

original.title: Selecting the principal inverse-cosh branch
original.question_html:
(a)[4]

Derive \(\cosh^{-1}x=\ln(x+\sqrt{x^2-1})\), stating the domain and explaining the choice of sign.

(b)[2]

(a)

Set \(y=\cosh^{-1}x\), where \(x\ge1\) and \(y\ge0\). Then \(2x=e^y+e^{-y}\). With \(u=e^y\ge1\),

\[u^2-2xu+1=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u=x\pm\sqrt{x^2-1}.\]

(b)

The domain is \(x+1\ge1\), or \(x\ge0\). Applying cosh gives \(x+1=\cosh(\ln4)=17/8\), so \(x=9/8\). This satisfies the domain.

original.title: Inverse tanh: logarithm and graph
original.question_html:
(a)[4]

Derive a logarithmic expression for \(\tanh^{-1}x\) and state its real domain.

(b)[3]

Sketch \(y=\tanh^{-1}x\), showing its asymptotes and intercept, and state its range and symmetry.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Express tanh using \(e^{2y}\), then solve for that exponential.

(b)

The graph is the reflection of \(y=\tanh x\) in \(y=x\).
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(\tanh^{-1}x=\frac12\ln\frac{1+x}{1-x}\), for \(-1<x<1\).

(b)

Asymptotes \(x=-1\) and \(x=1\); intercept \((0,0)\); range \(\mathbb R\); odd symmetry.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(y=\tanh^{-1}x\). Using the exponential form,

\[x=\frac{e^{2y}-1}{e^{2y}+1}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad (1-x)e^{2y}=1+x.\]

Hence

\[e^{2y}=\frac{1+x}{1-x},\qquad y=\frac12\ln\frac{1+x}{1-x}.\]

Tanh has range \((-1,1)\), so this is the inverse domain. Equivalently, the exponential quotient is positive precisely on this interval. The endpoints are not allowed.

(b)

The logarithm tends to \(-\infty\) as \(x\to-1^+\) and to \(+\infty\) as \(x\to1^-\). Thus both asymptotes are vertical. The function is increasing, is zero at 0, and is odd because replacing \(x\) by \(-x\) reciprocates the logarithm's argument. Its range is all real numbers.

Solve \(\sinh^{-1}x+\sinh^{-1}\frac34=\sinh^{-1}\frac43\), giving a rational answer.

(b)[2]

This is the inverse-sinh value obtained in part (a).

(a)[6]

(a)

Both inverse functions require \(-1/2<x<1/2\). On this interval all factors in the logarithmic expressions are positive, so

\[\ln\frac{(1+x)(1+2x)}{(1-x)(1-2x)}=\ln6.\]

\[x=\frac{21-\sqrt{241}}{20}\]

is the only real solution. Every transformation used was reversible on the stated domain.

original.title: Three inverse functions, one value
original.question_html:
(a)[4]

For \(x\ge1\), prove \(\cosh^{-1}x=\sinh^{-1}\sqrt{x^2-1}=\tanh^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{x^2-1}}{x}\right)\).

(b)[2]

original.hint_html:
(a)

Put \(u=\cosh^{-1}x\ge0\), then find sinh and tanh of \(u\).

(b)

\(\sqrt{(13/5)^2-1}=12/5\).
original.answer_html:
(a)

All three expressions equal the same nonnegative number \(u\).

(b)

Each expression equals \(\ln5\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(u=\cosh^{-1}x\ge0\). Then \(\cosh u=x\), and the fundamental identity gives \(\sinh u=\sqrt{x^2-1}\); the nonnegative root is needed because \(u\ge0\). Applying inverse sinh gives the first equality.

\[\cosh^{-1}\frac{13}{5}=\ln\left(\frac{13}{5}+\frac{12}{5}\right)=\ln5.\]

The other forms are \(\sinh^{-1}(12/5)=\ln5\) and \(\tanh^{-1}(12/13)=\tfrac12\ln25=\ln5\).

original.title: A discriminant is not enough
original.question_html:
For a real parameter \(k\), consider \(\cosh2x-k\cosh x+2=0\).

(a)[3]

With \(c=\cosh x\), reduce the equation to a quadratic and state the restriction on \(c\).

(b)[4]

Determine the number of distinct real solutions in \(x\) for every real \(k\). Explain why a discriminant calculation alone is insufficient.

(c)[2]

Find all real solutions when \(k=5\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

The range of cosh must accompany the quadratic.

(b)

Rearrange the quadratic as \(k=2c+1/c\) for \(c\ge1\).

(c)

Only the larger quadratic root is at least 1.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(2c^2-kc+1=0\), with \(c\ge1\).

(b)

No solutions if \(k<3\); one if \(k=3\); two if \(k>3\).

(c)

\(x=\pm\cosh^{-1}\left(\frac{5+\sqrt{17}}4\right)\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

The identity \(\cosh2x=2\cosh^2x-1\) gives

\[2c^2-1-kc+2=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad2c^2-kc+1=0.\]

Because \(c=\cosh x\), only roots with \(c\ge1\) can correspond to real \(x\).

(b)

For an admissible \(c\), rearrange to \(k=2c+1/c\). On \([1,\infty)\), this function increases strictly: for \(c_2>c_1\ge1\),

\[\left(2c_2+\frac1{c_2}\right)-\left(2c_1+\frac1{c_1}\right)=(c_2-c_1)\left(2-\frac1{c_1c_2}\right)>0.\]

Its value at 1 is 3 and it grows without bound. Thus \(k<3\) gives no admissible \(c\), \(k=3\) gives \(c=1\) and only \(x=0\), while \(k>3\) gives exactly one \(c>1\) and hence two opposite real \(x\)-values.

The discriminant \(k^2-8\) only decides whether the quadratic has real roots in \(c\); it does not impose \(c\ge1\) or count the two inverse-cosh branches.

(c)

The two quadratic roots are \((5\pm\sqrt{17})/4\). The smaller lies below 1; the larger exceeds 1. Therefore

\[x=\pm\cosh^{-1}\left(\frac{5+\sqrt{17}}4\right).\]

original.title: A rational hyperbolic substitution
original.question_html:
Let \(t=\tanh(x/2)\), where \(x\) is real.

(a)[4]

Show that \(\sinh x=\frac{2t}{1-t^2}\) and \(\cosh x=\frac{1+t^2}{1-t^2}\). State the range of \(t\).

(b)[4]

Use this substitution to solve \(3\cosh x-2\sinh x=4\), giving answers in logarithmic form.
original.hint_html:
(a)

First solve \(t=(e^x-1)/(e^x+1)\) for \(e^x\).

(b)

Check both quadratic roots against \(-1<t<1\), then use \(e^x=(1+t)/(1-t)\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

The exponential form gives

\[t=\frac{e^x-1}{e^x+1}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^x=\frac{1+t}{1-t}.\]

Also \(-1<t<1\), so the denominator and the exponential are positive. Therefore

\[\sinh x=\frac12\left(\frac{1+t}{1-t}-\frac{1-t}{1+t}\right)=\frac{2t}{1-t^2},\]
\[\cosh x=\frac12\left(\frac{1+t}{1-t}+\frac{1-t}{1+t}\right)=\frac{1+t^2}{1-t^2}.\]

(b)

Substitution gives

\[\frac{3(1+t^2)-4t}{1-t^2}=4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad7t^2-4t-1=0.\]

Hence \(t=(2\pm\sqrt{11})/7\), and both lie in \((-1,1)\). Using \(e^x=(1+t)/(1-t)\),

\[e^x=\frac{9\pm\sqrt{11}}{5\mp\sqrt{11}}=4\pm\sqrt{11}.\]

Both are positive. Taking logarithms gives the stated two solutions.

original.title: An inverse-function equation with a radical
original.question_html:
(a)[4]

Solve \(\cosh^{-1}(x+2)=2\sinh^{-1}\sqrt{x}\), showing that no extraneous solution has been introduced.

(b)[3]

More generally, determine all real \(a\) for which \(\cosh^{-1}(x+a)=2\sinh^{-1}\sqrt{x}\) has a real solution, and find the solution.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Both sides are nonnegative on their common real domain, so applying cosh is reversible there.

(b)

After applying cosh, also check both original domain requirements.
original.solution_html:
(a)

The square root requires \(x\ge0\), which also ensures \(x+2\ge1\). Both sides are nonnegative. Since cosh is one-to-one on \([0,\infty)\), the equation is equivalent to

\[x+2=\cosh\left(2\sinh^{-1}\sqrt x\right)=1+2x.\]

Thus \(x=1\). It lies in the domain. The identity \(\cosh(2u)=1+2\sinh^2u\) and the principal branches make the transformation reversible, so this solution is neither extraneous nor incomplete.

(b)

On the common domain \(x\ge0\) and \(x+a\ge1\), both sides remain nonnegative. Applying cosh yields \(x+a=1+2x\), hence \(x=a-1\). The first domain condition requires \(a\ge1\). For such \(a\), the second condition is also satisfied because \(x+a=2a-1\ge1\). Thus the condition is necessary and sufficient, and the solution is unique.

original.title: Challenge: a complete parameter classification
original.stem_html: For real \(a\), define \(F_a(x)=\cosh x-a\sinh x\) on \(\mathbb R\).
original.question_html:
For real \(a\), define \(F_a(x)=\cosh x-a\sinh x\) on \(\mathbb R\).

(a)[4]

For \(|a|<1\), write \(F_a(x)\) as \(R\cosh(x-b)\), where \(R>0\), and determine its minimum.

(b)[5]

For every pair of real numbers \(a,k\), determine the number of distinct real solutions of \(F_a(x)=k\). Include \(a=1\) and \(a=-1\).

(c)[2]

Find all solutions when \(a=3/5\) and \(k=1\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Compare \(R\cosh b\) and \(R\sinh b\) with 1 and \(a\).

(b)

For the remaining cases use \(F_a(x)=\frac{1-a}{2}e^x+\frac{1+a}{2}e^{-x}\).

(c)

The exponential equation factorises.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(R=\sqrt{1-a^2}\), \(b=\tanh^{-1}a\). The minimum is \(\sqrt{1-a^2}\), at \(x=\tanh^{-1}a\).

(b)

For \(|a|<1\), there are 0, 1 or 2 solutions according as \(k<\sqrt{1-a^2}\), \(k=\sqrt{1-a^2}\), or \(k>\sqrt{1-a^2}\).

For \(|a|=1\), there is one solution when \(k>0\) and none when \(k\le0\).

For \(|a|>1\), there is exactly one solution for every real \(k\).

(c)

\(x=0\) or \(x=\ln4\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

Expanding gives \(R\cosh b=1\) and \(R\sinh b=a\). Subtracting their squares yields \(R^2=1-a^2\), so \(R=\sqrt{1-a^2}>0\). Taking their ratio gives \(\tanh b=a\), hence \(b=\tanh^{-1}a\). Therefore

\[F_a(x)=\sqrt{1-a^2}\cosh(x-\tanh^{-1}a).\]

Its minimum is \(\sqrt{1-a^2}\), occurring only when \(x=\tanh^{-1}a\).

(b)

For \(|a|<1\), part (a) gives the three cases from the minimum of a shifted cosh curve.

If \(a=1\), \(F_a=e^{-x}\); if \(a=-1\), \(F_a=e^x\). Each is one-to-one with range \((0,\infty)\), so each gives one solution for \(k>0\) and none otherwise.

If \(a>1\), the coefficient of \(e^x\) is negative and that of \(e^{-x}\) positive. Both terms decrease strictly as \(x\) increases. Their sum tends to \(+\infty\) on the left and \(-\infty\) on the right. Continuity and strict decrease therefore give exactly one solution at every height. If \(a<-1\), both terms instead increase strictly and the limits are reversed, with the same one-solution conclusion. This includes all real \(a,k\).

For completeness, when \(|a|<1\), the number of distinct real roots is

\[\begin{cases}0,&k<\sqrt{1-a^2},\\1,&k=\sqrt{1-a^2},\\2,&k>\sqrt{1-a^2}.\end{cases}\]

(c)

With \(u=e^x>0\), the equation is \(u/5+4/(5u)=1\), or \(u^2-5u+4=0\). Thus \(u=1,4\), giving \(x=0,\ln4\). As a check, the minimum is \(4/5<1\), so two roots are expected.

original.title: Two positive roots and a limiting case
original.question_html:
(a)[3]

Using exponential definitions, prove \(\cosh2x=1+2\sinh^2x\).

(b)[4]

Find all real values of \(k\) for which \(\cosh2x+2=k\sinh x\) has two distinct positive real roots.

(c)[1]

When \(k=2\sqrt6\), find the single distinct real root.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Expand the square of \(e^x-e^{-x}\).

(b)

The quadratic roots must be both distinct and positive; a positive discriminant alone is not enough.

(c)

Use the repeated root of the quadratic in sinh.
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[1+2\sinh^2x=1+\frac12(e^x-e^{-x})^2=1+\frac12(e^{2x}-2+e^{-2x})=\frac12(e^{2x}+e^{-2x})=\cosh2x.\]

(b)

Put \(s=\sinh x\). The equation becomes \(2s^2-ks+3=0\). Since sinh is strictly increasing and \(\sinh0=0\), positive \(x\)-roots correspond exactly to positive \(s\)-roots.

The discriminant is \(k^2-24\), the product of the roots is \(3/2>0\), and their sum is \(k/2\). Thus the roots are distinct when \(|k|>2\sqrt6\), and both are positive exactly when also \(k>0\). Combining these conditions gives \(k>2\sqrt6\).

(c)

The repeated quadratic root is \(s=k/4=\sqrt6/2\). It corresponds to the single distinct value \(x=\sinh^{-1}(\sqrt6/2)=\ln((\sqrt6+\sqrt{10})/2)\).

original.title: An inverse-cosh antiderivative in a shifted equation
original.question_html:
In this question \(x>3\).

(a)[4]

For \(u>4\), show that \(F(u)=\frac u2\sqrt{u^2-16}-8\cosh^{-1}(u/4)\) satisfies \(F^{\prime}(u)=\sqrt{u^2-16}\).

(b)[8]

Solve \((x+1)\frac{dy}{dx}-y=2(x+1)^2\sqrt{(x+1)^2-16}\), given that \(y=10\) when \(x=4\). Give an explicit exact expression for \(y\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate both terms before combining the fractions.

(b)

An integrating factor is \(1/(x+1)\). Then use part (a) with \(u=x+1\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

The chain rule gives

\[\frac{d}{du}\cosh^{-1}\left(\frac u4\right)=\frac1{\sqrt{u^2-16}}.\]

By the product rule,

\[F^{\prime}(u)=\frac12\sqrt{u^2-16}+\frac{u^2}{2\sqrt{u^2-16}}-\frac8{\sqrt{u^2-16}}.\]

The last two terms combine to \((u^2-16)/(2\sqrt{u^2-16})\). Adding the first term yields \(\sqrt{u^2-16}\). The domain \(u>4\) ensures all derivative expressions are defined.

(b)

Divide by \(x+1>0\):

\[y^{\prime}-\frac{y}{x+1}=2(x+1)\sqrt{(x+1)^2-16}.\]

An integrating factor is \(e^{-\int dx/(x+1)}=1/(x+1)\). Therefore

\[\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{y}{x+1}\right)=2\sqrt{(x+1)^2-16}.\]

Putting \(u=x+1\) and using part (a),

\[\frac{y}{x+1}=(x+1)\sqrt{(x+1)^2-16}-16\cosh^{-1}\left(\frac{x+1}{4}\right)+C.\]

At \(x=4\), the radical is 3 and \(\cosh^{-1}(5/4)=\ln2\). The initial condition gives \(2=15-16\ln2+C\), so \(C=16\ln2-13\). Multiplication by \(x+1\) gives the stated explicit solution on \(x>3\). The initial point lies strictly inside this domain; the derivative identity is not asserted at its singular endpoint.

Final result

\(y=(x+1)\left[(x+1)\sqrt{(x+1)^2-16}-16\cosh^{-1}\left(\frac{x+1}{4}\right)+16\ln2-13\right]\).

original.title: Inverse sinh and a translated independent variable
original.question_html:
Throughout this question \(x>-2\).

(a)[4]

Use integration by parts to find \(\int\sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{x+2}{3}\right)\,dx\).

(b)[8]

Solve \((x+2)y^{\prime}-y=(x+2)^2\sinh^{-1}((x+2)/3)\), given \(y=8\) when \(x=2\). Give your answer in the form \(y=f(x)\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

First put \(u=x+2\). In the remaining integral, use \(d(\sinh^{-1}(u/3))/du=1/\sqrt{u^2+9}\).

(b)

Multiply the linear form by \(1/(x+2)\) and use part (a).
original.solution_html:
(a)

Set \(u=x+2\). Integrating by parts gives

\[\int\sinh^{-1}(u/3)\,du=u\sinh^{-1}(u/3)-\int\frac{u}{\sqrt{u^2+9}}\,du.\]

The last integral is \(\sqrt{u^2+9}\), as is seen by the substitution \(v=u^2+9\). Thus

\[\int\sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{x+2}{3}\right)dx=(x+2)\sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{x+2}{3}\right)-\sqrt{(x+2)^2+9}+C.\]

(b)

Division by \(x+2\) puts the equation in linear form,

\[y^{\prime}-\frac{y}{x+2}=(x+2)\sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{x+2}{3}\right).\]

The integrating factor is \(1/(x+2)\), valid on the stated domain. Therefore

\[\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{y}{x+2}\right)=\sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{x+2}{3}\right).\]

Using part (a),

\[\frac{y}{x+2}=(x+2)\sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{x+2}{3}\right)-\sqrt{(x+2)^2+9}+C.\]

When \(x=2\), \(\sinh^{-1}(4/3)=\ln3\) and the radical is 5. Hence \(2=4\ln3-5+C\), giving \(C=7-4\ln3\). Multiplying by \(x+2\) yields the required explicit solution.

Final result

\(y=(x+2)\left[(x+2)\sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{x+2}{3}\right)-\sqrt{(x+2)^2+9}+7-4\ln3\right]\).

original.title: A coth integrating factor and an endpoint limit
original.question_html:
In this question \(x>0\).

(a)[3]

Show that \(\frac{d}{dx}\ln(\operatorname{coth}x)=-2\operatorname{cosech}2x\).

(b)[6]

Solve \(\sinh2x\,y^{\prime}-2y=\sinh2x\), given \(y=8/5\) when \(x=\ln3\).

(c)[1]

Find \(\lim_{x\to0^+}y\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use \(\operatorname{coth}x=\cosh x/\sinh x\).

(b)

Part (a) identifies the integrating factor after division by \(\sinh2x\).

(c)

The logarithm diverges, but it is multiplied by a factor tending to zero.
original.solution_html:
(a)

On \(x>0\), coth is positive, so its logarithm is defined. Write

\[\ln(\operatorname{coth}x)=\ln(\cosh x)-\ln(\sinh x).\]

Differentiating gives \(\tanh x-\operatorname{coth}x=-1/(\sinh x\cosh x)=-2/\sinh2x\), as required.

(b)

The linear form is \(y^{\prime}-2\operatorname{cosech}2x\,y=1\). By part (a), an integrating factor is \(\operatorname{coth}x\). Hence

\[\frac d{dx}(y\operatorname{coth}x)=\operatorname{coth}x.\]

original.title: A scaled identity and long-run behaviour
original.question_html:
(a)[3]

Use exponential definitions to prove \(2\cosh^2(2x)=\cosh4x+1\).

(b)[6]

Solve \(y^{\prime}+4y\tanh(2x)=3\), given \(y=-1\) when \(x=0\).

(c)[2]

Find \(\lim_{x\to\infty}y\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Expand the square of \((e^{2x}+e^{-2x})/2\).

(b)

The integrating factor is \(\cosh^2(2x)\).

(c)

Use \(\sinh4x=2\sinh2x\cosh2x\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

Using the definition of cosh,

\[2\cosh^2(2x)=\frac12(e^{2x}+e^{-2x})^2=\frac12(e^{4x}+2+e^{-4x})=\cosh4x+1.\]

(b)

An integrating factor is

\[\exp\left(\int4\tanh(2x)dx\right)=\exp(2\ln\cosh2x)=\cosh^2(2x).\]

Thus \(\frac d{dx}(y\cosh^2(2x))=3\cosh^2(2x)\). Using part (a),

\[y\cosh^2(2x)=\frac32\int(\cosh4x+1)dx=\frac38\sinh4x+\frac32x+C.\]

At \(x=0\), the initial condition gives \(C=-1\). Dividing by the positive \(\cosh^2(2x)\) yields the stated solution, valid for all real \(x\).

Final result

\(y=\operatorname{sech}^2(2x)\left[\frac38\sinh4x+\frac32x-1\right]\).

(c)

Rewrite the solution as

\[y=\frac34\tanh2x+\left(\frac32x-1\right)\operatorname{sech}^2(2x).\]

The first term tends to \(3/4\). The second tends to zero because the reciprocal cosh-squared factor decays exponentially, faster than the linear factor grows. Hence the limit is \(3/4\).

original.title: Challenge: from a triple-angle identity to a differential equation
original.question_html:
(a)[4]

Prove from exponential definitions that \(\sinh3x=3\sinh x+4\sinh^3x\).

(b)[4]

Use \(u=\sinh x\) to find \(\int\sinh^2(3x)\cosh x\,dx\).

(c)[6]

Hence solve \(y^{\prime}+y\tanh x=\sinh^2(3x)\), given \(y=2\) when \(x=0\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Expand \((e^x-e^{-x})^3\) and combine with the linear term.

(b)

Part (a) makes the transformed integrand a polynomial in \(u\).

(c)

Multiply by \(\cosh x\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(u=e^x\). Then

\[3\sinh x+4\sinh^3x=\frac32(u-u^{-1})+\frac12(u-u^{-1})^3.\]

The cubic expansion is \(u^3-3u+3u^{-1}-u^{-3}\). The linear terms cancel, leaving \(\frac12(u^3-u^{-3})=\sinh3x\), proving the result.

(b)

With \(u=\sinh x\), \(du=\cosh x\,dx\), and part (a) gives \(\sinh3x=3u+4u^3\). Thus

\[\int\sinh^2(3x)\cosh x\,dx=\int(3u+4u^3)^2du=\int(9u^2+24u^4+16u^6)du.\]

Term-by-term integration gives \(3u^3+(24/5)u^5+(16/7)u^7+C\). Substituting back gives the stated antiderivative.

Final result

\(3\sinh^3x+\frac{24}{5}\sinh^5x+\frac{16}{7}\sinh^7x+C\).

(c)

The integrating factor is \(e^{\int\tanh x dx}=\cosh x\). Multiplication gives

\[\frac d{dx}(y\cosh x)=\sinh^2(3x)\cosh x.\]

Use part (b) to obtain

\[y\cosh x=3\sinh^3x+\frac{24}{5}\sinh^5x+\frac{16}{7}\sinh^7x+C.\]

At \(x=0\), \(\cosh0=1\) and \(\sinh0=0\), so \(C=2\). Divide by \(\cosh x>0\) to obtain the required solution for every real \(x\). Differentiating the product \(y\cosh x\) also gives a direct check of the equation.

Final result

\(y=\operatorname{sech}x\left[3\sinh^3x+\frac{24}{5}\sinh^5x+\frac{16}{7}\sinh^7x+2\right]\).
